nameStory: The Common Ink Cap gets its name from its remarkable ability to dissolve into a black, ink-like liquid as it ages - a process called deliquescence. In fact, people once actually used this natural 'ink' for writing! It's also called 'tippler's bane' because it has a dangerous reaction with alcohol that can make drinkers violently ill.
description: The Common Ink Cap is a fascinating fungus that literally melts away as it matures, turning from a solid mushroom into black liquid drops. When young, it has a grey-brown, bell-shaped cap that eventually flattens before dissolving from the bottom up. These medium-sized mushrooms typically grow in dense clusters and have thin, delicate flesh with a mild taste when fresh.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Starts bell-shaped and grey-brown, then flattens and begins dissolving into black liquid from the edges inward - this melting process is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White when young, quickly turning black and liquefying, creating dark droplets that fall from the mushroom

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows in tight clusters or clumps, never alone - look for multiple mushrooms sprouting from the same base

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: White to pale grey, hollow inside with a smooth texture, and remains relatively intact even as the cap dissolves

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a mild, pleasant mushroom odor with no unpleasant or chemical scents

habitat: Common Ink Caps love disturbed, nutrient-rich soils and are often found in urban areas like lawns, vacant lots, compost piles, and along roadsides. They're saprophytic, meaning they feed on decaying organic matter in the soil. You'll frequently spot them in grassy areas where the ground has been enriched with organic debris.

seasonality.spring: Begins fruiting after warm spring rains, especially in May and June when soil temperatures rise and moisture is abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Common Ink Caps, appearing in flushes 1-3 days after heavy rains throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting through early fall, often producing some of the largest clusters of the year during September and October.
seasonality.winter: Dormant period with no visible fruiting bodies, though the underground mycelium remains active in unfrozen soil.

funFact: This mushroom contains a compound called coprine that acts like the anti-alcoholism drug Antabuse - if you drink alcohol within 72 hours of eating it, you'll experience severe nausea, racing heart, and other unpleasant symptoms that can last for hours!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Shaggy Mane (Coprinus comatus), but Shaggy Manes are taller, pure white when young, and have a distinctive shaggy, scaly cap surface. Remember: Common Ink Caps are grey-brown and smooth, Shaggy Manes are white and shaggy.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'inky cap,' this species was recently moved from the genus Coprinus to Coprinopsis based on DNA studies. You may still see it listed under its old name Coprinus atramentarius in older field guides, which can be confusing for beginners trying to look it up.
compareHints: Among New England's ink caps, the Common Ink Cap is distinguished by its grey-brown color and urban habitat preferences. The Hare's Foot Inkcap is much smaller and more delicate, while the Scaly Ink Cap has distinctive scales on its cap surface. The Magpie Inkcap is larger and has distinctive black and white patches, making it quite different in appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its inkcap relatives, hare's foot inkcap is distinguished by its small size, extremely short lifespan, and fuzzy white appearance when young.

Among New England's ink caps, the scaly ink cap stands out for its felt-like cap scales, while the hare's foot ink cap is much smaller and more delicate, and the common ink cap has a smooth, grayish cap without scales.
